entities.name: National Gallery of Canada
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa is the country's premier art museum, founded in 1880 and now housed in a striking Moshe Safdie building of glass and granite since 1988. With over 75,000 works spanning Canadian, Inuit, and international art, it is the most visited museum in Canada's capital and houses the world's largest collection of Canadian art, including key works by the Group of Seven.

Founded by the Marquess of Lorne in 1880 to encourage the fine arts in Canada, the gallery moved several times before commissioning architect Moshe Safdie for its permanent home on Sussex Drive. Safdie's design of geometric glass pavilions — inspired by crystal structures and connected indoor gardens — created one of Canada's most celebrated public buildings. The exterior's glass-encased neo-Gothic arcade mirrors the adjacent Parliament buildings.

The gallery's collection reflects Canada's complex identity: European masters (Rembrandt, El Greco, Rubens) alongside Indigenous and Inuit art galleries that present centuries of non-European artistic traditions; the Group of Seven's defining Canadian landscape paintings; and contemporary international art including the controversial 1990 purchase of Barnett Newman's Voice of Fire for $1.76 million (Canadian), which sparked a national debate about public arts funding. The museum holds the only Raphael painting in the Western Hemisphere.
